FINAL SETTLEMENT DECISION NOTICE
Pursuant to Rule 108 of the Audit Enforcement Procedure

This Final Settlement Decision Notice is a document prepared by Executive Counsel
following an investigation relating to the Respondents. It does not make findings
against any persons or entities other than the Respondents and it would not be fair to
treat any part of this document as constituting or evidencing findings against any other
persons or entities since they are not parties to the proceedings.

INTRODUCTION
1.1
The Financial Reporting Council (the “FRC”) is the competent authority for Statutory
Audit in the United Kingdom and operates the Audit Enforcement Procedure (the
“AEP”), revised in June 2023. The AEP sets out the rules and procedure for the
investigation, prosecution and sanctioning of breaches of “Relevant Requirements”.
1.2
The AEP contains a number of defined terms and, for convenience, those defined
terms are also used within this document. Where defined terms are used, they appear
in italics.
1.3

1.4
This Final Settlement Decision Notice is issued pursuant to Rule 108 of the AEP in
respect of the conduct of:
(i)
Ernst & Young LLP (“EY”) the Statutory Audit Firm of the Group for the
FY17 and FY18 Audits.
(ii)
Mr Richard Wilson (“Mr Wilson”) a partner in EY at the Relevant Time and
the Statutory Auditor responsible for the FY17 and FY18 Audits. Mr Wilson
signed the FY17 and FY18 Audit Reports1 on behalf of EY.
1.5
In this Final Settlement Decision Notice, EY and Mr Wilson are referred to as the
“Respondents”.
1.6
In accordance with Rule 102 of the AEP, Executive Counsel entered into settlement

1.7
A Proposed Settlement Decision Notice was issued by Executive Counsel on 11

Final Settlement Decision Notice pursuant to Rule 107(a) of the AEP.

2.
BACKGROUND
2.1
The Group described itself as “one of the world’s leading travel groups”2 (comprising
traditional travel agent services and an airline) and, as at September 2019, operated
from 16 countries, with 21,000 employees. The Company’s shares were listed on the
main market of the London Stock Exchange.
2.2
In 2011, the Group suffered a loss in bookings which was attributed to disruption in
the Middle East/African region. The Group required an additional £200 million loan
from its bankers to fund a shortfall in cashflow.
2.3
In 2012/2013 the Group commenced a transformation project to reform the business
and move it towards profitable growth. In 2015, the Group refinanced its existing
borrowings.
2.4
In 2016, the Group suffered a fall in bookings which was attributed to overseas
terrorist attacks in the previous year3.
FY17
2.5
FY17 was EY’s first year of auditing Thomas Cook.
2.6
The FY17 Financial Statements were signed on 21 November 2017. The Group
Income Statement reported revenue of £9.007 billion, gross profit of £1.993 billion
and profit after tax for the year of £12 million. The Company’s Group Balance Sheet
reported total assets of £6.615 billion, total liabilities of £6.335 billion, and therefore
net assets of £280 million. Audit materiality was set at £15 million.
2.7
The FY17 Financial Statements accounted for £2.6 billion of Goodwill. This
represented 40% of the Group’s total assets and was the largest single item on the
balance sheet. As a result, a misstatement in the Goodwill balance had the potential
to be very large (as the Audit Team appreciated). Goodwill was not subject to any
impairment in FY17.
2.8
The FY17 Independent Auditor’s Report (“FY17 Audit Report”) signed by Mr Wilson
was unmodified. The FY17 Audit Report disclosed the carrying value of Goodwill as

statements” that was considered by the Audit Committee in the FY17 Corporate
Governance Report, although it was not treated as a significant audit risk by the

2.9
Note 12 to the FY17 Financial Statements included disclosures about Goodwill and
the impairment testing of Goodwill by Thomas Cook. The note explained that
impairment testing was performed by comparing the carrying value of each cash-
generating unit (“CGU”) to the recoverable amount, determined on the basis of the
CGU’s Value In Use (“VIU”). In summary, this involved comparing the value attributed
to the CGU’s assets to the future cashflows expected to be derived from using those
assets.
2.10
The Group divided its business into four CGUs for this purpose (which were also
adopted as its operating segments for the purpose of segmental reporting4). These
CGUs were UK Tour Operator (“UKTO”); Northern Europe Tour Operator (“NETO”);
Continental Tour Operator (“CETO”); and Group Airlines (“GAS”). The FY17 Financial
Statements were the first occasion on which these CGUs were adopted for the
Group’s financial reporting.
2.11
Note 4 to the FY17 Financial Statements explained that during the year the Group
had refined its organisational structure, resulting in a reassessment of its reportable
segments. Previous financial statements had reported segments on a geographical
basis (UK, Northern Europe, Continental Europe and Condor5). The major change
effected by the re-organisation was that the Group’s airline business was treated as
a separate CGU from FY17, rather than being split geographically.
FY18
2.12
During 2018, the Group issued a series of profit warnings to the London Stock
Exchange (31 July 2018, 24 September 2018, and 27 November 2018). The Group
attributed its poor financial performance to a heatwave in Northern Europe and the
collapse of two major airlines in Germany.
2.13
On 24 September 2018, the Group also announced that its CFO would step down
from the Board on 30 November 2018.

The Revised Business Plan was approved by the Board on 27 November 2018. The
Group concluded, in light of the Revised Business Plan and its updated FY18 year-

2.16
Around this time, and in order to mitigate against a future breach, the Group pursued
a reset of its banking covenants for Q1/Q2 FY19 and Q1/Q2 FY20.
2.17
In late October/early November 2018 a partner in EY’s Restructuring Department
(“the Restructuring Partner”) and a manager in that same team (“the
Restructuring Manager”) (together the “Restructuring Team6”) joined the Audit
Team. Prior to EY tendering for the Group’s FY17 Audit, the Restructuring Partner
had been Global Client Service Partner for the Group, a role that they had held from
2014 until Mr Wilson assumed this role on commencement of the FY17 Audit.7 The
Respondents engaged the Restructuring Team to assist with the audit of Going
Concern. The output of this work, which included an analysis of the forecast covenant
and liquidity headroom with sensitivities and a review of management’s assumptions,
represented a substantial part of the FY18 Audit work performed on Going Concern.
2.18
Between 2 October 2017 and 28 November 2018, the Company’s share price fell by
70% from 121.7p to 36.08p per share.
2.19
Given issues identified with the Group’s forecast covenant compliance, the Audit
Team considered whether a material uncertainty existed which could cast significant

2.20
The covenant resets referred to at paragraph 2.16 were agreed by the banks in late
November 2018, shortly before the signing date of the FY18 Independent Auditor’s
Report (“FY18 Audit Report”).
2.21
The FY18 Financial Statements were approved for issue on 28 November 2018. The
Group Income Statement reported revenue of £9.584 billion, gross profit of £1.933
billion and a loss after tax for the year of £(163) million. The Group Balance Sheet
reported total assets of £6.569 billion, total liabilities of £6.278 billion, and therefore
net assets of £291 million. Audit materiality was set at £14 million.
2.22
The FY18 Financial Statements accounted for £2.6 billion of Goodwill. This
represented 39% of the Group’s total assets and was still the largest single item on
the balance sheet. Goodwill was not subject to any impairment in the FY18 Financial
Statements.
2.23
The FY18 Audit Report was signed by Mr Wilson on 28 November 2018. It was
unmodified and noted no material uncertainty relating to the use of the Going Concern
assumption.
2.24
As with the FY17 Audit, the Respondents did not consider Goodwill to be a
‘Significant Risk.’ The Respondents initially did not consider Going Concern to be a
‘Significant Risk’ but it was upgraded to a ‘Significant Risk’ in early November 2018.
Goodwill and Going Concern were included as ‘Key Audit Matters’ in the FY18 Audit
Report. They were also included as “significant issues in relation to the financial
statements” that were considered by the Audit Committee in the FY18 Corporate
Governance Report.
2.25
Note 12 to the FY18 Financial Statements included a sensitivity analysis for the
UKTO CGU, which held £1 billion of the £2.6 billion Goodwill balance. It disclosed
that a reasonably possible change in the UKTO CGU future cash flows would result
in the CGU’s carrying amount exceeding the VIU8. The note also stated that the VIU

FY 2019
2.26
The Group continued to fall short of its forecasts. On 7 February 2019, Thomas Cook
confirmed that it had commenced a strategic review of its airline business.
2.27
The Group’s interim financial statements for the six months ended 31 March 2019
were issued on 16 May 2019. Performance had still not improved. Sales were lower
than forecast and down relative to the equivalent point in FY18. The Group sustained
an underlying first-half loss on an earnings before interest and tax basis of £245m.
The Group prepared revised forecasts for the full year, taking account of performance
to date. These revised forecasts reduced the expectations for the performance of the
UKTO business and the directors of Thomas Cook decided to fully impair Goodwill in
the UKTO CGU as at 31 March 2019, resulting in Goodwill being written down from
over £1 billion to zero.
2.28
The interim financial statements also included a ‘Material Uncertainty Related to
Going Concern’ paragraph in EY’s Independent Review Report. The revised
forecasts had shown that the Group would require additional liquidity to continue
trading. Although a £300m nine month bridging facility was agreed in principle with
the Group’s banks, it was not executed when the interim financial statements were
issued. The directors recognized that there was uncertainty surrounding the outcome
of the strategic review and this new financing arrangement and concluded that these
matters could cast significant doubt on the ability of the Group to continue as a Going
Concern.
2.29
On 12 July 2019 the Group reported that it was pausing its strategic review and would
not be proceeding with a sale of its airline or tour operator business. It also reported
that it was pursuing a recapitalization plan involving £750 million of new money. The
Group progressed the recapitalization plan during July and August 2019 and agreed
key terms with the relevant parties during this period. Ultimately however, the Group
was unable to secure agreements with key stakeholders. The Group’s directors
subsequently concluded on 22 September 2019 that Thomas Cook was insolvent
and should be placed into compulsory liquidation with immediate effect.
2.30
The liquidation of Thomas Cook resulted in approximately 9,000 redundancies, the
closure of over 500 retail stores and over 1,000 companies and government entities

10
being owed money. Over 140,000 customers had to be repatriated to the UK, at an
estimated cost of £83 million to the taxpayer.

3.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
3.1
As noted above, the Statutory Audit Firm and Statutory Auditor responsible for the
FY17 Audit and FY18 Audit were EY and Mr Wilson respectively. In this regard:
(i)
In 2017, EY was ranked as the fourth largest audit firm in the UK, with audit
revenues of £442 million and 116 audit principals. In 2018, EY’s audit
revenues were £458 million and it had 115 audit principals.
(ii)
In 2017, Mr Wilson was a partner of EY, with over 30 years’ statutory audit
experience. His focus in the 15 years prior to the FY18 Audit was on FTSE
100 companies where he acted as the lead audit partner.
(iii) The FY17 Audit was the first audit for which EY and Mr Wilson were,
respectively, the Statutory Audit Firm and Statutory Auditor of the Group.
3.2
The Respondents’ statutory responsibility was to form an opinion as to whether the
FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements showed a true and fair view and had been
properly prepared in accordance with the Companies Act 2006 and Applicable
Accounting Standards (including IAS 1: Presentation of Financial Statements
(“IAS 1”) and when accounting for Goodwill, IAS 36: Impairment of Assets (“IAS
36”)). The Relevant Requirements applicable to the FY17 Audit and FY18 Audit
include the International Standards on Auditing (“ISAs”) and the Ethical Standard
2016.
3.3
As set out in this Final Settlement Decision Notice, there were serious failings in the
manner in which the FY17 and FY18 Audits were performed. The breaches of
Relevant Requirements in this Final Settlement Decision Notice relate to
inadequacies in two fundamental areas of audit work (which occurred over two
separate audit years in respect of (i) and (ii) below), and in relation to one overarching
principle (see (iv) below):
(i)
The auditing of the Group’s impairment testing of Goodwill during the FY17
Audit (“Goodwill FY17”).
(ii)
The auditing of the Group’s impairment testing of Goodwill during the FY18
Audit (“Goodwill FY18”).
(iii) The auditing of the Company’s Going Concern Assessment during the
FY18 Audit (“Going Concern FY18”).

12
(iv) The failure to adequately consider a risk to EY’s independence during the
FY18 Audit and the application of safeguards (“Independence FY18”).
3.4
Ultimately, as a result of the Respondents’ breaches of Relevant Requirements, in
the areas of Goodwill (for FY17 and FY18) and Going Concern (for FY18) both of the
FY17 and FY18 Audits failed in their principal objective: that of providing reasonable
assurance that the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements were free from material
misstatement.
3.5
The applicable Relevant Requirements and the Respondents’ breaches of Relevant
Requirements in relation to the FY17 and FY18 Audits are described in more detail
in sections 4 and 5 of this Final Settlement Decision Notice. However, in summary
the breaches concern:
(i)
A lack of sufficient appropriate audit evidence - An auditor is required
to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence (as defined in ISA 500) to
be able to draw reasonable conclusions about the amounts and
disclosures in the financial statements in order to give reasonable
assurance that the financial statements are free from material
misstatement, whether caused by fraud or error. The Respondents failed
to obtain sufficient evidence to support and adequately corroborate certain
key assumptions and estimates which were included in management’s
assessments of (in FY17 and FY18) Goodwill impairment and (in FY18)
Going Concern.
(ii)
A lack of professional scepticism - An auditor is also required by ISA
200.15 to “plan and perform an audit with professional scepticism
recognizing that circumstances may exist that cause the financial
statements to be materially misstated…the auditor shall maintain
professional scepticism throughout the audit, recognising the possibility of
a material misstatement due to facts or behaviour indicating irregularities,
including fraud, or error, notwithstanding the auditor's past experience of
the honesty and integrity of the entity's management and of those charged
with governance.” Professional scepticism includes consideration of the
sufficiency and appropriateness of audit evidence obtained in the light of
the circumstances. The Respondents accepted without adequate
challenge that there was significant headroom on each of the CGUs and
that because of that headroom, the impairment testing was not particularly

13
sensitive to changes in the assumptions being made by Thomas Cook. In
respect of Going Concern the Respondents failed to challenge
management adequately on their forecasting accuracy, sensitivity testing
and on the level of liquidity headroom.
(iii) Inadequate disclosure in the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements –
The information presented in the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements in
relation to Goodwill was not fully reliable and understandable as required
by the applicable financial reporting framework.
(iv) The failure to adequately consider a risk to EY’s independence during
the FY18 Audit – The Restructuring Partner’s long association with the
Group and longstanding and close business relationship with the CFO (as
a result of past work on behalf of EY), amounted to a “Familiarity threat”9
which created a risk to EY’s independence within the meaning of the
Ethical Standard 2016. The Respondents failed to take sufficient steps to
ensure that the Restructuring Partner’s long association with the Group
and senior members of the finance team was properly considered. In so
doing they also failed properly to evaluate whether additional safeguards
were required.
(v)
A failure to prepare sufficient audit documentation - This failure is
evident in all four areas of the Audit summarised at (i) to (iv) above.
3.6
As the Senior Statutory Auditor responsible for the FY17 and FY18 Audits, Mr Wilson
was responsible for the overall quality of the Audits and the direction, supervision,
and performance of the Audits in compliance with the professional standards and
applicable legal and regulatory requirements. Accordingly, Mr Wilson is responsible
for all breaches of Relevant Requirements in relation to the FY17 and FY18 Audits.
3.7
Further as the Statutory Audit Firm responsible for the Audit, EY is responsible for all
breaches of Relevant Requirements on the part of its partners or employees.
3.8
It should be noted that:
(i)
Whilst this Final Settlement Decision Notice identifies and explains failings
in the Respondents’ audit work it does not assert that any balances or
amounts were in fact misstated. However, there was information available

Goodwill balance for the UKTO may have been impaired. Whilst the audit
work conducted to assess Going Concern was inadequate – in that the
Respondents did not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence in order
to be able to conclude on whether a material uncertainty existed - and
breached Relevant Requirements, it is not alleged that there was in fact a

(ii)

A financial sanction of £6,500,000, discounted for admissions and early

(ii)
A published statement in the form of a Severe Reprimand;
(iii) A declaration that the FY17 and FY18 Audit Reports signed on behalf of

(iv) An order to take action to prevent recurrence of the breaches as detailed

Against Mr Wilson:
(i)
A financial sanction of £140,000, discounted for admissions and early

5.
BREACHES OF RELEVANT REQUIREMENTS
A.
Goodwill FY17
Background
5.1
The £2.6 billion of Goodwill included in the Group’s balance sheet arose
predominantly from mergers with MyTravel Group plc, Thomas Cook AG and Co-op
Travel, and from the Company’s acquisition of Condor from Lufthansa.
5.2
Goodwill arises on the acquisition of one business by another. Under IFRS 3, the
acquirer has to assess the value of the assets and liabilities it has acquired. The
identifiable assets and liabilities can include items that may not have been on the
acquiree’s balance sheet, such as the brand name. The residual amount paid by the
acquirer over and above the value of those assets and liabilities is recognised in the
group financial statements as Goodwill. It is an intangible asset that represents: “the
future economic benefits arising from other assets acquired in a business
combination that are not individually identified and separately recognised11.”
5.3
When accounting for Goodwill (post-acquisition), the Group was required to apply
IAS 36. IAS 36 explains (1) assets are to be carried at no more than their recoverable
amount, which is the amount that can be earned from selling or using the asset (i.e.
the value in use or VIU (see paragraph 2.9 above)), and (2) if the carrying value is
greater than the recoverable amount, it is described as “impaired” and an impairment
loss is recognised in the financial statements. For assets such as Goodwill, where
the recoverable amount cannot be determined at the individual asset level (because
Goodwill does not generate cashflows independently of other assets) the recoverable
amount is determined at the level of the CGU12 (which is the smallest group of assets
that generate cashflows independently of other assets).
5.4
Note 12 to the FY17 Financial Statements (Intangible Assets) stated that the Group
assessed Goodwill impairment by comparing the carrying value (“CV”) of each CGU’s
assets and liabilities to the VIU (i.e. cashflows) expected to be generated by the
CGUs in the future.
5.5
The Group’s VIU calculations for the purpose of its impairment testing were based on
assumptions in the FY18-FY21 business plan (the “FY18-FY21 Business Plan”)

Background
5.82
The Going Concern assumption is fundamental to the preparation of financial
statements and a key consideration for any Statutory Auditor to address. The
principal accounting standard that Thomas Cook was required to apply was IAS 1:
Presentation of Financial Statements. IAS 1 requires management to make an
assessment of an entity’s ability to continue as a Going Concern. It also states that
an entity shall prepare its financial statements on a Going Concern basis unless
management intends to liquidate the entity or to cease trading, or has no realistic
alternative but to do so. This requirement applies even when there are uncertainties
about events or conditions that may cast significant doubt upon the entity’s ability to
continue as a Going Concern in the future. Such uncertainties are required to be
disclosed in the financial statements when they are material.
5.83
In considering whether a company/group is a Going Concern, the key test is therefore
whether the company/group can pay its debts as they fall due for a period of not less
than twelve months from the date the financial statements are approved. If the Going
Concern assumption is not appropriate, the company/group prepares its accounts on
a break-up basis, with assets valued on the basis of expected realisation from a
forced sale.
5.84
IAS 1 explains that: (1) when management is aware, in making its Going Concern
assessment, of material uncertainties related to events or conditions that may cast
significant doubt upon the entity's ability to continue as a Going Concern, the entity
shall disclose those uncertainties44; and (2) when an entity has a history of profitable
operations and ready access to financial resources, the entity may reach a conclusion
that the Going Concern basis of accounting is appropriate without detailed analysis.
In other cases, management may need to consider a wide range of factors relating
to current and expected profitability, debt repayment schedules and potential sources
of replacement financing before it can satisfy itself that the Going Concern basis is
appropriate45.
5.85
Sensitivity testing, stress testing and scenario analysis are mechanisms used to
assess the risks facing a business and the potential impacts if those risks were to

Nature, seriousness, gravity and duration of the breaches
6.6
The breaches of Relevant Requirements feature serious audit failings in two
important areas of the financial statements: Goodwill (for FY17 and FY18) and Going
Concern (for FY18). As a result, both the FY17 and FY18 Audits failed in their
principal objective: to provide reasonable assurance that the FY17 and FY18
Financial Statements were free from material misstatement.
6.7
The Goodwill balance amounted to £2.6 billion and comprised approximately 40% of
the Group’s total assets for both FY17 and FY18. It was therefore necessary that the
Respondents approached this audit area with sufficient scepticism in order to properly
challenge and corroborate the assumptions and estimates in support of
management’s Goodwill impairment model. Regrettably, that did not happen in either
of the FY17 or FY18 Audits. The failings for the audit of Goodwill in FY18 are
particularly serious given Thomas Cook’s deteriorating trading performance, which
presented the heightened risk that the Goodwill balance for the UKTO CGU may have
been impaired.

6.8
Going Concern in FY18 was rightly identified as a significant audit risk, however the
procedures performed by the Respondents in response were inadequate and there
were serious audit failings as a result. The Respondents failed to adequately
challenge management with regards to sensitivity testing and liquidity headroom and,
on the basis of the evidence obtained, they were not in a position to properly conclude
on whether a material uncertainty existed. Given the known issues concerning
Thomas Cook’s forecasting accuracy and liquidity headroom, significant further work
should have been performed by the Respondents, particularly in light of Thomas
Cook’s deteriorating financial performance and the issues identified with its forecast
covenant compliance.
6.9
The Relevant Requirements breached embraced the entire audit process in the areas
of Goodwill impairment and Going Concern and included areas such as risk
assessment, the performance of procedures as to obtaining and evaluating audit
evidence, communication with those charged with governance and disclosures. They
feature breaches of key auditing standards dealing with the exercise of professional
scepticism, partner supervision and audit documentation which are central to the
performance of an audit. The failings also include a failure to adequately consider a
risk to independence. The Relevant Requirements breached were thus extensive and
important.
6.10
It is not asserted that the FY17 or FY18 Financial Statements were in fact misstated,
however as a result of the breaches of Relevant Requirements set out in this Final
Settlement Decision Notice the Respondents failed to obtain reasonable assurance
that the FY17 and FY18 Financial Statements were free from material misstatement.
It is therefore asserted that there was at least the risk that the Financial Statements
were materially misstated.
6.11
Paragraphs 2.26 to 2.30 above summarise the events that occurred following the
FY18 Audit. The Group issued interim financial statements for the six months ended
31 March 2019 on 16 May 2019 in which the Group prepared revised forecasts for
the full year and the directors of Thomas Cook decided to fully impair Goodwill in the
UKTO, resulting in Goodwill of over £1 billion being written off. The financial
statements also included a ‘Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern’
paragraph in EY’s Independent Review Report.
6.12

Statements would have been presented differently absent the breaches, including

therefore be the case that the information presented to stakeholders when the FY18
Financial Statements were published in December 2018 would have been the same
even if the audit work had been performed in accordance with Relevant

following their audit work in the key areas of Goodwill impairment and Going Concern,

stakeholders in circumstances where, absent the breaches, stakeholders might have
been in possession of information regarding Material Uncertainty and Goodwill
impairment earlier than 16 May 2019 which could have enabled them to take different
decisions in the interim to achieve a more favourable outcome.

confidence in the truth and fairness of published financial statements. Whilst the

The core audit failings relating to the impairment of Goodwill, a key audit area, were
